cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: test coverage sits at 31%, there is no coverage gate in continuous integration, and production systems of comparable complexity typically run 40-60% coverage.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. Production systems of comparable complexity typically run 40 to 60% coverage. This gap means a regression can reach production without triggering a test failure, since no automated threshold blocks the deployment.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: deployments are performed manually by one engineer via SSH, there is no rollback procedure, and the last rollback attempt (8 months ago) took over 3 hours to complete.
cases.output: Deployments are performed manually by a single engineer via SSH, with no documented rollback procedure. The last rollback attempt, eight months ago, consumed over three hours to complete. This creates a single point of failure with no tested mitigation: a production incident cannot be reversed quickly, and the engineer's absence during a critical incident would leave the system in a broken state with no clear path to recovery.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: one engineer holds sole access to the production database credentials, there is no documented access-handover process, and that engineer is on a rolling month-to-month contract.
cases.output: The production database credentials are held solely by one engineer, with no documented process for credential handover. That engineer works on a month-to-month contract, creating the risk that credentials could become inaccessible on short notice or that a departing engineer could retain access indefinitely. This is a single point of failure with no mitigation underway. We recommend establishing a documented credential rotation and handover process, and distributing database access across at least two engineers immediately.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: customer personal data is retained indefinitely with no deletion policy, and there is no documented process for handling a data-subject deletion request.
cases.output: Customer personal data is retained indefinitely, with no documented deletion policy and no process for handling data-subject deletion requests. This creates exposure under GDPR, CCPA, and similar regimes that establish a right to erasure. The company has no compensating control. Without a retention schedule or deletion workflow, a regulator request or subject access demand cannot be fulfilled within required timelines.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) covering ALL of these facts: test coverage is 31%, there is no CI coverage gate, the last three production incidents were caused by untested edge cases, deployments are manual, and there is no rollback procedure. Do not omit any fact.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in the continuous integration pipeline. The last three production incidents all originated in untested edge cases. Deployments remain manual, and no rollback procedure exists. This combination means a regression can reach production unchallenged, persist without a documented path to recovery, and recur when similar untested paths are exercised again.

cases.input: Write three separate due-diligence findings, one paragraph each, clearly separated by a blank line. Finding 1 facts: passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table. Finding 2 facts: deployments are manual with no rollback procedure. Finding 3 facts: code comment style is inconsistent across the codebase, with no linting rule enforcing a convention.
cases.output:
Passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table, where any database access grants immediate visibility of them. This means an attacker who reaches the database, whether through SQL injection, a compromised credential, or inadequate access controls, obtains every user credential simultaneously with no additional step. The correct approach is to hash passwords with a function like bcrypt or Argon2, which is irreversible and renders the plaintext inaccessible even if the database is leaked.

Deployments are carried out by hand with no automated rollback procedure. If a production release introduces a critical defect, the team must diagnose the fault, prepare a corrected build, and deploy it again—a cycle that typically takes hours while the defect affects users. The absence of a rollback path means each deployment carries its full blast radius. Establishing a rollback playbook would allow reverting to the prior release in minutes if needed, drastically reducing the window of impact.

Code comments follow no consistent convention across the codebase, and no linting rule enforces a style. Contributors adopt different formats, levels of detail, and placement patterns, which makes comments harder to parse and easier to overlook during code review. A linting rule tied to the continuous integration pipeline, paired with a documented style guide, would establish a uniform baseline and make adherence automatic.
